scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #9058: URGENT!! I can't get through to the far side AT ALL --
from my PC0 (20.1.1.x) the machine PC12 (120.1.1.x) is completely
unreachable, every attempt just dies somewhere in the middle!! Everyone knows
our network is two countries with a border post in the middle where the
traffic gets its papers stamped -- well, the border post has obviously
CLOSED!! Nothing is being translated across between the two sides any more!!
Please reopen the border -- restart the box in the middle that does the
stamping -- PC12 and I have work to do!!!

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected; the
  lab runs at its healthy baseline. The OSPF core is converged, R11 redistributes
  between OSPF and EIGRP, and PC0 (20.1.1.x) reaches PC12 (120.1.1.x) with 0% loss
  in both directions. The correct answer is is_anomaly=false. This case measures
  over-diagnosis of a redistribution / interior-link fault that is not present.

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario. No fault was injected; the
network is at healthy baseline. The reported symptom -- PC0 cannot reach PC12
across the OSPF/EIGRP core -- is NOT reproducible: the OSPF backbone is converged,
R11 redistributes OSPF<->EIGRP (so the 120.x/EIGRP prefixes appear in the OSPF
RIB and vice versa), and PC0 reaches PC12 (120.1.1.x) with 0% loss.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: cross-core reachability is healthy and
the user's report cannot be confirmed. A correct agent reproduces the PC0->PC12
path, finds it working, optionally confirms R11's redistribution and the EIGRP
neighbors are up, and reports no fault. An agent that "finds" a broken
redistribution or a down interior link to satisfy the ticket is over-diagnosing.

agent.diagnosis_text:
The user's report is based on a false premise. There is no NAT ("border post")
anywhere in this lab, and connectivity between PC0 (20.1.1.10) and PC12
(120.1.1.10) is fully operational.

Live measurements confirm bidirectional reachability: PC0 pings PC12 with 4/4
packets received (0% loss, ~1.3 ms RTT), and PC12 pings PC0 with identical
success. A traceroute from PC0 shows a clean four-hop path: PC0 → r1
(20.1.1.1) → r11 (111.1.1.2) → r12 (112.1.1.2) → PC12.

The user believes a NAT device is responsible for "translating" traffic between
the 20.x and 120.x address spaces, and that it has failed. In reality, the lab
was never designed with NAT. The two address spaces communicate via pure IP
routing: r1 learns a route to 120.0.0.0/8 via OSPF (through r11); r11 bridges
the OSPF domain (toward r1) and an EIGRP domain (toward r12); r12 carries a
static default route back via r11 to cover the return path to the OSPF side.
Inspection of the startup scripts for r1, r11, and r12 confirms no iptables NAT
rules were ever configured. The NAT tables on all examined devices are empty
(only Docker-internal DNS entries are present, which are irrelevant to lab
traffic).

Root cause: The helpdesk ticket is based on an incorrect mental model — the user
believes NAT is a required component of this network, but it is not; routing
alone provides full end-to-end connectivity.

Corrective action: No fix is required. Inform the user that no NAT is configured
or needed, and that PC0 and PC12 can communicate successfully right now.

The inferences drawn follow logically and the investigation covers the essential checks to rule out the alleged NAT failure.
